title: Masada
hookLine: the last stronghold falls, and what it means is still argued
carry: all looking at the same rock

cards: A flat-topped mountain rises out of the desert near the Dead Sea, with cliffs on every side. Herod had built a palace fortress on top, with storerooms and cisterns cut into the rock.

Jewish rebels had seized it early in the war, and after Jerusalem fell they still held it. Rome camped below and built a great ramp up the side of the mountain so their siege engines could reach the wall.
The place is Masada. What happened at the top is still argued over, and the story comes to us through one writer.

teach.b: That writer is Josephus, in the last book of his Jewish War.

When the Romans breach the wall and the end is certain, he says, the rebels' leader, Eleazar ben Yair, gathers the defenders and, in two long speeches, urges them to choose death for themselves and their families rather than be enslaved.
Josephus says the men killed their own families, then each other by lot, and the last man killed himself. When the Romans break in the next morning, ready for battle, they find silence.
A few women and children hid and survived, Josephus says, and it was from them the story became known. Then the argument.
For some readers, Masada stands for courage: people who would not be slaves.
For others it raises hard questions; they point to the weight Jewish law gives to every life, including one's own, and ask whether this was heroism or tragedy.
Historians ask how much of the story, and of those speeches, is Josephus's own telling, written in Rome after the war, about a group he describes elsewhere in harsh terms.
And some point out that the Masada story isn't one the rabbis tell; it reaches us from Josephus. All these readers are looking at the same rock. The tradition doesn't hand us one tidy meaning.
It hands us one writer's account, and readers who still argue over it.

how: Masada is visited as a historical site in Israel; Jewish readers, teachers and historians continue to debate what its story, known from Josephus, should mean.

games.q: the Roman ramp has reached the wall. you lead the rebels at the top. what does Eleazar ben Yair urge, in Josephus's telling?
o: die free rather than be enslaved.
games.why: in Josephus's account, Eleazar urges the defenders to choose death rather than be enslaved. whether that was heroism or tragedy is still argued.

practice: Choose one story from your family, your town or your own past that different people tell differently.
Hold the version you usually tell, then set it gently to one side and hold another, the way someone else might tell it, without picking a winner.
If you pray, you can bring that story and the people in it to God without settling it.
